spans.assertion: the dataset used comprised 146,028 player-referee dyads from the 2012-2013 European soccer season
the primary analysis defined light skin as rating 0-0.25 and dark skin as rating 0.75-1.0 and compared these two groups
the primary comparison sample comprised 100,527 dyads from 1,255 players and 2,805 referees
the adjusted risk difference for dark- vs light-skinned players was +0.22pp (95% CI -0.06 to 0.51; p=0.125) and was not statistically significant at α=0.05
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.168 (95% CI 0.971 to 1.404; p=0.099)
a sensitivity analysis using continuous skin tone across all players found a 0.30pp increase per unit (95% CI 0.02 to 0.57; p=0.035), statistically significant
the hypothesis is concluded not supported based on the primary estimand, since the CI includes zero and p exceeds 0.05, despite a small positive point estimate
the unit of analysis was chosen as the player-referee dyad
590 dyads with missing height/weight data were excluded, leaving N=99,937 dyads for the primary model
the primary model used 1,239 unique players as clusters
the outcome was operationalized as a binary indicator for whether the player received at least one red card from that referee
exposure was defined as dark skin (1) versus light skin (0)
light skin was defined as average rating ≤0.25, yielding N=89,611 dyads from 1,123 players
dark skin was defined as average rating ≥0.75, yielding N=10,326 dyads from 132 players
the middle skin-tone category (0.25-0.75) was excluded from the primary analysis to create a clearer contrast
a linear probability model with cluster-robust standard errors (clustered at player level) was used
the model was specified with dark skin, games, height, weight, position, and league as predictors of red card probability
number of games in the dyad was included as a covariate, treated as a critical exposure variable
player position was included via 11 dummy variables, with Attacking Midfielder as reference
league country was included via 3 dummy variables, with England as reference
height and weight were included as continuous covariates
the adjusted risk difference was +0.22pp (95% CI -0.06 to 0.51; p=0.125)
after adjustment, dark-skinned players had a 0.22pp higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players, not statistically significant, with a CI including zero
the baseline (light skin) red card rate was 1.22%
the unadjusted dark-skin red card rate was 1.42%
the 0.22pp difference represents an 18% relative increase over baseline
with 95% confidence the true difference could range from -0.06pp to +0.51pp
logistic regression with the same covariates as the primary model was used for the secondary estimand
the logit model was specified with dark skin, games, position, league, height, and weight as predictors

the LPM with cluster-robust SE was treated as the conservative primary estimate
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.168 (95% CI 0.971 to 1.404; p=0.099)
the odds of a red card for dark-skinned players were 16.8% higher, not statistically significant, CI includes 1.0, and this is consistent with the risk-difference finding
each observation represents a player-referee pair counting total red cards across all their encounters
the complete-case analysis included 99,937 dyads
1,239 unique players were used as the cluster variable
the sample included 2,805 unique referees
games was included as a critical confounder/exposure variable because more games means more opportunity for red cards

spans.note: Sensitivity and Robustness Checks section heading

spans.assertion: all players with skin tone data (N=123,868 dyads, 1,564 players) were used, treating skin tone as continuous
the risk difference was +0.30pp per full unit increase in skin tone (95% CI 0.02 to 0.57; p=0.035)
this continuous-skin-tone result was significant at α=0.05
the continuous result suggests a possible dose-response relationship, though it may be driven by differences not captured in the binary comparison
without height/weight the risk difference was +0.24pp (95% CI -0.05 to 0.52; p=0.105)
this result is nearly identical to the primary result, so height/weight do not substantially affect the estimate

raters: two independent coders blind to research question
scale: 5-point scale from very light to very dark

spans.note: red card data source: official match records

red card counts were aggregated to the dyad level across all games between a player and referee

running the provided code on the original dataset will exactly reproduce all reported estimates to the stated precision

spans.assertion: the analysis of 99,937 dyads found an adjusted risk difference of +0.22pp (95% CI -0.06 to 0.51; p=0.125)
the hypothesis is concluded not supported
the 95% CI includes zero (no effect)
the p-value (0.125) exceeds the conventional 0.05 threshold
the point estimate suggests a small positive association but uncertainty is too large to rule out chance
the continuous-skin-tone sensitivity analysis showed a statistically significant effect (p=0.035), suggesting a possible dose-response relationship the binary comparison lacks power to detect

the analysis employed rigorous methods (cluster-robust SE, covariate adjustment, complete-case analysis, multiple sensitivity analyses) and based its conclusion on the pre-specified primary estimand following conventional inference standards
the final verdict is that the data do not provide sufficient evidence that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players
